nameStory: The Triangle Floater gets its name from the distinctive triangular shape of its shell, which is most pronounced in younger specimens. The 'floater' part refers to how these freshwater mussels can actually move around the river bottom, unlike their marine cousins that cement themselves to rocks. Early naturalists were fascinated by these 'floating' shells they'd find along riverbanks.
description: The Triangle Floater is a freshwater mussel that lives buried in the sandy or muddy bottoms of rivers and streams throughout New England. Its shell has a characteristic triangular outline when viewed from the side, with the pointed end facing forward. These medium-sized mussels typically grow 2-4 inches long and have brownish-green shells with subtle ridge patterns. Like all freshwater mussels, they're filter feeders that help keep our waterways clean by straining tiny particles from the water.

idTips.label: Triangular Shell Shape
idTips.description: The shell forms a distinct triangle when viewed from the side, with the pointed 'beak' (umbo) positioned toward the front third of the shell. This triangular profile is most obvious in younger specimens.

idTips.label: Shell Surface Texture
idTips.description: Feel for subtle, wavy ridges (undulations) running across the shell surface - these give the species its scientific name 'undulata'. The shell feels slightly rough under your fingertips, not smooth like a pond mussel.

idTips.label: Color Pattern
idTips.description: Living shells are typically brownish-green to olive with darker growth rings. Dead shells you find on shore often fade to chalky white or pale yellow, but may still show faint green rays.

idTips.label: Size Range
idTips.description: Adults measure 2-4 inches long, making them medium-sized among New England's freshwater mussels. They feel surprisingly heavy for their size when picked up.

idTips.label: Interior Shell Color
idTips.description: Open shells reveal a pearly white to pale pink interior with a smooth, lustrous feel. The muscle scars (where the animal attached) are clearly visible as darker oval marks.

habitat: Triangle Floaters prefer clean, flowing rivers and larger streams with sandy or fine gravel bottoms throughout New England's lowlands and foothills. They're often found in areas with moderate current where they can filter-feed effectively, typically buried 1-2 inches deep in the substrate. Look for their shells along riverbanks after spring floods, especially in the Connecticut, Merrimack, and Penobscot river systems.

seasonality.spring: Spring floods often wash empty shells onto riverbanks, making this the best time to find specimens for identification. Living mussels become more active as water temperatures warm.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when mussels are actively filter-feeding and reproducing. Living specimens are most likely to be found partially exposed on sandy river bottoms during low water periods.
seasonality.fall: Mussels begin to burrow deeper as temperatures drop. Fresh shells from natural mortality may be found along shorelines after autumn rains and higher water levels.
seasonality.winter: Mussels remain buried deep in sediment, largely inactive. Ice-out conditions in late winter may reveal shells frozen in shallow areas or along ice-scoured banks.

funFact: Triangle Floaters are essentially living water purifiers - a single adult can filter over 10 gallons of river water per day, removing bacteria, algae, and pollution particles that would otherwise cloud the water and harm fish habitat.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with Brook Floaters, but Triangle Floaters have a more pronounced triangular shape and wavy surface ridges, while Brook Floaters are more oval and smoother. Memory trick: 'Triangle' has more angles, just like the shell shape and surface texture.
contextualKnowledge: Freshwater mussels are among North America's most endangered animals, with many species declining due to dam construction, pollution, and habitat loss. Finding shells doesn't necessarily mean living populations exist nearby - mussels can live 20-50 years, so old shells may persist long after populations disappear.
compareHints: Triangle Floaters are more angular than their Brook Floater cousins, which have rounder, more oval shells with smoother surfaces. The Elktoe, another relative, is much larger (up to 5 inches) and has a more elongated shape rather than the Triangle Floater's compact triangular form. The wavy ridges on Triangle Floater shells are also more pronounced than on either relative.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Brook floaters are smaller and prefer cleaner, smaller streams compared to their relatives the triangle floater and elktoe, which can tolerate larger rivers and slightly more disturbed conditions.
Unlike the Triangle Floater which has a more angular, triangular shell shape, the elktoe is more evenly oval.
